title: Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
description: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders
wiki_lead:
Ehlers–Danlos syndromes (EDS) are a group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders. Symptoms often include loose joints, joint pain, stretchy, velvety skin, and abnormal scar formation. These may be noticed at birth or in early childhood. Complications may include aortic dissection, joint dislocations, scoliosis, chronic pain, or early osteoarthritis.
It occurs due to mutations in one or more of the 19 particular genes which can contribute to the condition. The specific gene affected determines the type, though the genetic cause of hypermobile Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (hEDS) are still unknown. Some cases result from a new variation occurring during early development. In contrast, others are inherited in an autosomal dominant or recessive manner. Typically, these variations result in defects in the structure or processing of the protein collagen or tenascin. Diagnosis is often based on symptoms, particularly hEDS, but people may initially be misdiagnosed with somatic symptom disorder, depression, or myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome. Genetic testing is used to confirm all types of EDS except hEDS, for which a genetic marker has yet to be discovered. The classification was updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms added.
A cure is not known, and treatment is supportive in nature. Several medications can help improve symptoms, such as pain and blood pressure drugs, which reduce joint pain and complications caused by blood vessel weakness. Some forms have a normal life expectancy, but those that affect blood vessels generally decrease it.
While EDS affects at least one in 5,000 people globally, other types occur at lower frequencies. The prognosis depends on the specific type. Excess mobility was first described by Hippocrates in 400 BC. The syndromes are named after two dermatologists, Edvard Ehlers and Henri-Alexandre Danlos, who detected symptoms at the turn of the 20th century.

Types
In 2017, 13 subtypes of EDS were classified using specific diagnostic criteria. According to the Ehlers–Danlos Society, the syndromes can also be grouped by the symptoms determined by specific gene mutations. Group A disorders are those that affect primary collagen structure and processing. Group B disorders affect collagen folding and crosslinking. Group C includes disorders of the structure and function of the myomatrix. Group D disorders are those that affect glycosaminoglycan biosynthesis. Defects in the complement pathway characterize Group E disorders. Group F are disorders of intracellular processes, and Group G is considered to be unresolved forms of EDS.


Classical
Classical EDS is characterized by extremely elastic skin that is fragile and bruises easily, and hypermobility of the joints. Molluscoid pseudotumors (calcified hematomas that occur over pressure points) and spheroids (cysts that contain fat occurring over forearms and shins) are also often seen. grok_lead: EhlersâDanlos syndromes (EDS) are a heterogeneous group of inherited connective tissue disorders caused by variants in genes involved in the structure, production, or processing of collagen, leading to weakened support in the skin, joints, blood vessels, bones, and internal organs. These conditions manifest with a wide range of symptoms, from mild joint hypermobility and skin hyperextensibility to severe complications such as vascular rupture and organ fragility, depending on the subtype. The overall prevalence of EDS is estimated at least 1 in 5,000 individuals worldwide, though the hypermobile type is the most common, affecting approximately 1 in 5,000 to 20,000 people. In 2017, an international consortium classified EDS into 13 distinct subtypes based on clinical features, inheritance patterns, and genetic causes, with the classical, hypermobile, and vascular types being the most recognized. The classical EDS is characterized by skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and generalized joint hypermobility, often inherited in an autosomal dominant manner due to mutations in COL5A1 or COL5A2 genes. Hypermobile EDS, the most prevalent form, features joint instability, chronic pain, and soft, velvety skin without a definitively identified genetic marker in all cases, though it is typically autosomal dominant. The vascular EDS, considered the most severe, arises from mutations in the COL3A1 gene and predisposes individuals to life-threatening arterial or organ ruptures, easy bruising, and characteristic facial features such as a thin nose and prominent eyes. Common symptoms across subtypes include overly flexible joints prone to dislocations, fragile skin that bruises easily and heals with widened scars, and muscle fatigue, though severity varies widely. Diagnosis typically involves clinical evaluation using criteria like the Beighton score for joint hypermobility, family history assessment, and confirmatory genetic testing, as there is no single laboratory test for all forms. Management is supportive and multidisciplinary, emphasizing physical therapy to stabilize joints, protective measures to prevent injury, wound care to minimize scarring, and regular monitoring for cardiovascular risks in vascular subtypes, with no curative treatment available. Genetic counseling is recommended for affected individuals and families to understand inheritance risks and reproductive options.
